Each frame is a different artist's world (hand/heart on volcanic ridge, glowing peak, glass-and-amber figure, textile/mesh field, glass-tube knot with red cluster). This is the festival-titles format of many studios under one umbrella, credited per artist ('Boldtron', 'Medusa Lab').
The materials are rich and deliberate: subsurface skin, frosted glass, woven mesh, fibrous strands and caustic-tinted metal, with backlight and rim light that have a source.
The palettes differ from frame to frame but are each chosen with care: salmon/clay, violet dusk, sky blue with amber, sage with blush, bottle green with ice blue.
The custom OFFF MX wordmark is cut into geometric blocks and sits against the organic forms. It is a real identity, not a default.
Studio names are set as small bold-sans captions. They work as labels and have no expressive role.
gaps: There is no shared visual or motion thread linking the segments. B builds one camera grammar and one mechanical metaphor across the whole piece; A reads as a showreel of separate pieces.
Type has no role apart from the logo. Credits are dropped in the top-left like captions instead of being placed inside the 3D space, as B does with its sigils and map labels.
The organic, grotesque-surreal 3D language is already familiar from festival titles. A narrative or structural idea is needed to lift it beyond strong look development.

tells: The idea belongs to this piece alone: the world map is a clockwork model that builds itself, so the show's geography and politics become mechanism. It works as the exposition device for the series.
Light is motivated by an armillary sun. The engraved astrolabe band glows hot, and the miniature cities sit in tilt-shift light with smoke.
Materials are tactile and crafted: worn brass, carved wood, parchment map, bone-white spires, gears.
Typography is a custom-feeling inscribed serif, small and integrated. Each credit carries a house sigil and sits on the terrain. The title lockup is cast into the metal band.

The frames show real choreography: astrolabe, then aerial flight across the map, then cities rising, then map labels, then the title ring closing the loop. The motion has weight and spatial continuity.
gaps: The palette is mostly warm brass and sepia with grey-green. A colder secondary accent could separate regions more clearly.
Credits are very small against busy detail, so legibility depends on shallow depth of field.
The title card repeats the opening astrolabe band. Ending on an unexpected image would add a last surprise.

tells: The idea is specific and witty: every credit is a cigarette pack of its own invented brand, so the titles carry the film's satire of tobacco marketing.

The typography is a catalogue of period packaging lettering: ribbon-banner condensed slab, brush script, Didone 'LIGHTS', art-deco caps, italic script with heavy grotesk. Each choice is right for its fake brand.
The colours are pulled from real packaging history (royal blue with gold, orange with cream, red/white/blue stripe, menthol green, Marlboro red), all with aged-paper warmth.
Scanned-print texture and details such as tax stamps, 'underage sale prohibited' microcopy, eagles, crests and the bloodhound engraving show deep art direction.
Motion is implied by tight crops and pans across flat pack art, ending on the reveal of a row of filters.
gaps: The motion is mostly flat 2D pans across printed surfaces. B has a dimensional camera and assembly choreography, and D lacks that spatial depth.
Light is flat scan light. Some real physical lighting on foil, cellophane or embossing would add material richness.
Every frame follows the same crop-a-pack format. One structural surprise in the middle, such as a change of scale or a pack opening, would vary the rhythm.

tells: Dense, layered organic 3D: translucent subsurface hands, knitted mesh, fibrous hair, glassy tubes with beaded clusters. These are deliberately mixed material vocabularies, not stock primitives
Lighting is motivated and varies by shot: a dusk rim on the black terrain, a volcanic plume against a violet sky, a backlit blue cyclorama for the glass figure

Each frame is a different world with its own palette (rose/umber, violet/black, cerulean, sage/coral, bottle green), which reads as a festival-ident anthology with several artists (OFFF-style 'Boldtron', 'Medusa Lab' credits)
The custom stencil-like OFFF MX wordmark shows a real identity layer
gaps: Typography is an afterthought. The artist credits are default bold sans dropped in the top-left corner and never interact with the image; integrate type into the material worlds the way B's credits sit in the map
No through-line idea links the segments. It reads as a reel of beautiful renders, not one film with a thesis; it needs a governing concept or transition logic
The organic-surreal 3D look is very much of its moment. Push toward a stranger, more specific visual premise that only this festival could own

tells: A singular idea that only this piece could have: the world as a clockwork map, with cities that mechanically unfold. It doubles as narrative orientation for the episode
Real material and light: tooled leather and brass, an astrolabe band with engraved dragon reliefs, a blazing sun core, worn parchment terrain, tilt-shift depth
Credits are integrated into the world with sigil glyphs and engraved small caps set on the map. The custom wordmark is lit by the same light as the set
Choreography is evident across frames: the astrolabe flyover, a city rising from the board, then a map-scale move and the logo reveal on the sphere band. It works as a bookended structure
gaps: This is the benchmark entry; the remaining gaps are marginal
Tiny credits on busy map textures sometimes fight for legibility
The palette leans heavily on warm sepia. A little more cold contrast in the North could sharpen the geographic storytelling

tells: The concept is pitch-perfect and specific to the film: every credit is a period cigarette pack, a satire of tobacco branding delivered through tobacco branding

Typography with a point of view: each card uses a different, era-correct packaging style (ribbon banner with crest, script with bird-dog vignette, 'LIGHTS' serif with stars and stripes, deco menthol caps with palm and airplane, red brush script over rows of filters)
A deliberate vintage palette of royal blue, orange, red and green against warm cream, with print texture and misregistration feel
Jokes are hidden in the margins ('Underage sale prohibited', 'Honey-toasted', 'Premium blend'), so it rewards rewatching
gaps: Mostly flat scanned-print surfaces. Add physical light, foil sheen and cellophane so the packs feel like objects, as B's materials do
Motion is implied as crops and pans across flat artwork. It needs more camera and choreographic variety between cards
The structure is one card per name; a stronger escalation or narrative arc across the sequence would lift it from clever to unforgettable

defects: At 100%, tiles caught mid-shuffle leave thin slivers and misregistered fragments along their edges (right side of crop): the slip looks like a broken composite, not a deliberate offset
A stray tile fragment or smudge stays next to 'Lisboa' in the final settled frame, so the lockup does not resolve cleanly
Scattered tile shards break up the top-centre of the yellow pattern in frame 4, and they read as noise rather than a planned beat
The opening frame is almost empty cream tiles with one patterned tile: it is weak as a poster and close to dead air
The cream title plate is a blocky plus-shaped cluster that sits on the pattern without shadow or integration; it looks pasted on, not built from the tiles
Tile lighting is a flat, uniform sheen with no real glaze specular or falloff that changes as tiles move
gaps: The motion vocabulary is one move: tiles slide along the grid. The pairs show even, linear-looking slides with no anticipation, overshoot or settle weight per tile, and no change of scale or camera. The blue-to-yellow palette change is the only variation, and energy peaks around 50% instead of building to a 60-80% climax

The pattern does not build the logo. The 'Offset' title arrives on a separate plate instead of tiles slipping or rotating to form the letterforms, so the offset idea stops at the payoff. Top studio work would make the final slip produce the type

Finish and sound polish: transition frames show sliver and misregistration artifacts and the end frame has a leftover blemish. The soundtrack is a well-built pluck build and riser, but its hits sit on a steady grid rather than on each tile event, the 11s glitch sparkle is generic, and the tail is a static pad with no designed final hit or resolve on the logo
